- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.

- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.

- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him back

item.title: The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths [pdf]
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

For context, OpenAI's 4 new papers resolve 8 problems of the Top 500 Open Problems in Math list (LLM ranked, https://proofatlas.ai/open-problems/).

They include: #25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture.

#89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for #64 — Mean-payoff games, #65 — Parity games, #340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games.

#183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes, #130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart.

#137 — Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. For every fixed number of petals r, the paper proves the conjectured Cᵣᵏ bound.

(rankings post Riemann (#2) and VP vs VNP (#31)).

item.description:
Source: buttons.joshwcomeau.com

Top Comment:

The discussion about the value of sound in cars is especially interesting, but there is a further point behind it. That In Real Life We humans are adapted to use sound, not because we find it pleasant but because it tells us something about our environment. If you are old like I am, you know the real sound that a turn signal makes. It was caused as a electric relay repeatedly opened and closed. Now that sound is just an artifact (like roll up the window). But it is incredibly disturbing to hear the click stop when some other sound needs to play in my car while I am making a turn.

My conjecture is that we drastically underestimate the importance of using "sensory complete" interfaces. So yeah. A button should click.

item.title: 1Password Security Incident
item.description:
Source: 1password.com

Top Comment:

This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.

In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.

Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.

So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.

I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

item.title: GTA 6 Running on Windows
item.description:
Source: twitter.com

Top Comment:

For the general picture: the Xbox version of the game was leaked by Cyberleek - first the resources, then the game binary.

Because modern Xbox is very close to a Windows PC with some extra Xbox stuff, running the actual game code isn't hard, it's mostly about compatibility and graphics, plus the binary doesn't have any special DRM/obfuscation.

The current projects (xcl and VIctory) basically take a Wine-like approach. The main problems they have to solve, as I understand:

- The game ships with raw RDNA 2 shaders, so the projects have to translate that to another format, e.g. DXIL for DirectX 12, and compile those shaders. So you need a good translation/recompilation pipeline, if it's bad, the shaders will be bloated and perform poorly

- Xbox has unified memory, while most PCs do not, so you have to add a lot of workarounds and book-keeping for the game to work properly with that

- Xbox's DirectX 12 differs from the normal Windows one in some ways, and the game uses Xbox-specific texture formats with DirectStorage

I just wanted to share this because there's a lot of misconceptions going around about this being a "recomp" or something like that. Decompiling the entire binary (it's about 100MB of real executable machine code) will be a much bigger effort than getting this binary to run.

item.title: Ask HN: Anthropic is accusing my company of distilling. How can I prove I'm not?
item.description:
Source: news.ycombinator.com

Basically the title.

Anthropic is accusing me and my company of using their API for distillation. We are not. We do not train our own models.

Our only usage which I think could get us flagged is automated regression benchmarks whenever we change some AI settings. But this is not against their policy?

Now I've got 24h to prove we didn't.

Has anyone dealt with this too? How can you prove that you are not distilling Anthropic models without breaking your user's privacy?

Top Comment:

This happened to me with oai, and I only found out bc of a truly bizarre billing issue and reaching out to friends who were at the company. It took a lot of digging but it turned out they suspected me of distillation and just... didn't tell me.

Not saying it's what you should do, but here's what I would do. Basically show you're a good actor and you want to work with them.

1) rotate your keys, and tell them. if your keys were compromised (and lots of keys are) somebody out there COULD be distilling and you would be an "accessory" to it. letting them know that you're rotating JIC is good-actor behavior.

2) don't try to prove something you can't prove. as many have pointed out, there's no way to demonstrate that you aren't distilling.

3) ask for your day in court. tell them you want to use their models and want to clear this up, and ask them to provide you with whatever evidence they have (even if all they can give you is a date range or whatever!) so that you can analyze & respond.

if they won't play ball, sucks but tbh it's a big LLM world out there and you have lots of options!

item.title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed
item.description:
Source: www.lesswrong.com

Top Comment:

This shared LV cache thing is, in my mind, ridiculous. Web browser developers learned, quite a while ago, that caches need to be separated for different origins. Inference servers should add a similar feature: allow API calls to specify cache separation keys that prevent one security context from probing another context’s cache.

As for the step size issue, Google recently had a post about producing exactly consistent output across different kernels (specifically by defining a deterministic prefill algorithm and then requiring all kernels to generate results exactly equal to prefilling on the sequence in question).

More broadly, I think it’s a bit odd to frame this as “models” communicating. This is software communicating, and the models happen to be running the software.

item.title: Windows Loudness Equalization, reverse-engineered and ported to PipeWire
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

Interesting for audio nerds: Windows actually has an audio limiter. If you playback audio via loopback shared WASAPI, DirectSound or MME it actually gets compressed very slightly as it nears the peaks. The same does not happen via WASAPI exlcusive or ASIO.

Playing loudly mastered audio out of your PC will be very slightly different from the true audio source by about -0.1dbps with the compressor affecting the peaks.

It works via audiodg.exe (CAudioLimiter in AudioEng.dlll) on the shared-mode render path after all the streams get mixed, even if there's just one playing currently. This is necessary because two loud signals being mixed together might clip your DAC and that sounds nasty, so it's understandable that it's there.

Why would you care though? I was building a audio metering system to monitor audio via loopback and the properties of the audio I played in were being modified by the limiter in these normal modes. Maybe audio purists might not enjoy it either.

item.title: The short age of dragon riders
item.description:
Source: atilloy.com

Top Comment:

It's a well written article, but I disagree with it completely. It doesn't seem entirely internally cohesive. First, he says this:

> As of November 2026, the best public models still lack research taste. They execute beautifully when given a clear goal but are worse than the best researchers at coming up with good questions, or at having the sparks of creativity needed to get out of a dead end. They do not have as much vision as the best humans.

I agree! But then, apparently through the magic of RLVR, he somehow thinks that models will someday suddenly accrue this taste.

Why hasn't that happened yet? I get just as frustrated when I let Fable 5.2 make product decisions as I did with ChatGPT4. They solve the problems I give them much better, but when I try to let them lead to the next milestone, they consistently choose the worst, most conservative option.

> To do great things, we need to forgo some understanding of what is going on at lower levels, to focus on higher ones

If we don't understand the lower levels, how will we ensure that the "research taste" is good? How will we have any idea whether we are pushing towards the right kind of discoveries? It doesn't make any sense!

You can pretend that this is the same as something like my day job as a web developer. I don't fully understand how the hardware works at an atomic level. However, I have found that every time I learn more about the foundations on which my abstractions are built, I make better decisions in my job even though that knowledge is technically unnecessary. Understanding pointers in C finally made me understand object references in JavaScript, and it helped me to write more efficient code.

We need to understand what's happening underneath to some degree if we're going to build on top of it prudently.
